questionText:
Let $p$ and $q$ be two propositions. Consider the following two formulae in propositional logic.

$$S_1 : (\neg p \land (p \lor q)) \rightarrow q$$
$$S_2 : q \rightarrow (\neg p \land (p \lor q))$$

Which one of the following choices is correct?
options: $S_1$ is a tautology but $S_2$ is not a tautology.
$S_1$ is not a tautology but $S_2$ is a tautology.
explanation:
Evaluating Formula $S_1$:
$S_1: ( eg p \land (p \lor q)) ightarrow q$
Using the distributive law on the antecedent:
$ eg p \land (p \lor q) \equiv ( eg p \land p) \lor ( eg p \land q)$
Since $( eg p \land p) \equiv ext{False}$, this simplifies to:
$ ext{False} \lor ( eg p \land q) \equiv eg p \land q$

Substituting back into $S_1$:
$( eg p \land q) ightarrow q \equiv eg ( eg p \land q) \lor q$
$\equiv (p \lor eg q) \lor q \equiv p \lor ( eg q \lor q) \equiv p \lor ext{True} \equiv ext{True}$
Since $S_1$ evaluates to $ ext{True}$ under all truth assignments, $S_1$ is a tautology.

Evaluating Formula $S_2$:
$S_2: q ightarrow ( eg p \land (p \lor q))$
Simplifying the consequent:
$ eg p \land (p \lor q) \equiv eg p \land q$
So, $S_2 \equiv q ightarrow ( eg p \land q)$

Consider the truth assignment where $p = ext{True}$ and $q = ext{True}$:
Antecedent: $q = ext{True}$
Consequent: $ eg ext{True} \land ext{True} = ext{False} \land ext{True} = ext{False}$
Implication: $ ext{True} ightarrow ext{False} = ext{False}$

Since $S_2$ can evaluate to $ ext{False}$, $S_2$ is not a tautology.

Hence, $S_1$ is a tautology but $S_2$ is not a tautology.
